subject: ELA
overview: Read the assigned text before your child does whenever possible, and read many selections aloud together — discussion is the heart of this course. Each lesson pairs reading or writing with a short grammar or vocabulary focus; insist on text evidence ('What line tells you that?') in every answer. Writing units move from planning to drafting to revision over 1–2 weeks, so keep drafts in a folder and conference briefly on one or two goals at a time. Parental-preview notes flag mature moments (especially in Hatchet).

weeks.prep: Gather: 'Rikki-Tikki-Tavi' by Rudyard Kipling (from The Jungle Book), reading journal. Print or download 'Rikki-Tikki-Tavi' (in The Jungle Book on Project Gutenberg). Read it yourself first: the snake fights are suspenseful but not graphic.
misconceptions: Writing a 'quote sandwich' with no explanation. After every quote, the child must add a sentence beginning 'This shows…'.
Using objective pronouns as subjects ('Him and me went'). Test by dropping the other person: 'Me went' sounds wrong, so it's 'He and I went'.

days.guide: Help the child set up the notebook (reading-history page, a section for vocabulary). Read the first third aloud together, pausing when Nag appears so the child writes a prediction about the cobras.

questions.q: What is Rikki-tikki, and how does he come to live with Teddy's family?
questions.a: He is a young mongoose; a summer flood washes him out of his burrow, and Teddy's family finds him and revives him.

days.guide: Finish the story. Model one claim + quote + explain sentence set about Rikki ('Rikki is curious. The family motto is "Run and find out." This shows…'), then the child writes three traits with evidence.

questions.q: Name a trait of Rikki and support it with an event from the story.
questions.a: Brave: he attacks Nag in the bathroom and holds on even as he is thrown about; curious: he follows the motto 'Run and find out'; protective: he kills Karait near Teddy.

days.guide: Draw the plot mountain with the child labeling exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution. Ask: 'Which moment had you most worried?'

questions.q: What is the climax of the story? Defend your choice.
questions.a: Most readers choose Rikki following Nagaina down into the rat-hole: we don't know if he will come out alive. (Accept the Nag fight with a reason, but the final Nagaina battle resolves the main conflict.)

questions.q: Name one way Kipling builds suspense.
questions.a: Examples: Nag and Nagaina plotting in the dark; Darzee's wife distracting Nagaina; Nagaina threatening Teddy at breakfast; the long silence after Rikki goes down the hole.

days.guide: Teach the three cases with a chart (I/me/my, he/him/his, we/us/our, they/them/their). Model the 'drop the other person' test, then the child corrects 15 sentences and finds 5 story pronouns.

questions.q: Correct: 'Him and me went to the garden.'
questions.a: 'He and I went to the garden.'

questions.q: Correct: 'Teddy's mother gave the egg to my sister and I.'
questions.a: '…to my sister and me.' (object of the preposition)

days.guide: The child writes the paragraph independently, then takes the 10-item pronoun quiz.

questions.q: How is Rikki different at the end of the story than at the beginning?
questions.a: At first he is a curious, inexperienced young mongoose who has never fought a cobra; by the end he has defeated Karait, Nag and Nagaina and is the confident protector of the garden.

weeks.assessment_key: Evidence paragraph (4 = clear claim about how Rikki changes, e.g., from a curious, untested young mongoose to a confident, battle-proven protector; two accurate quotations — e.g., the family motto 'Run and find out' early, and the closing line that he 'had a right to be proud of himself'; each explained; 3 = claim and quotes but thin explanation; 2 = one quote or retelling only; 1 = no evidence). Pronoun quiz sample: 1) He and I 2) her and me 3) between you and me 4) We students 5) us kids 6) whom/who → 'Who is calling?' 7) My brother and I 8) to Teddy and me 9) theirs 10) its.

weeks.prep: Gather: 'The Ransom of Red Chief' and 'After Twenty Years' by O. Henry, 'The Open Window' by Saki. All three stories are on Project Gutenberg. Read 'The Open Window' first yourself so you can enjoy the twist with your child.
misconceptions: Confusing irony with coincidence. Irony is the gap between what is expected and what actually happens.
Thinking a twist ending is 'random'. Have the child find the clues (foreshadowing) on a second read.

days.guide: Read 'The Ransom of Red Chief' (aloud is fun). The child makes an Expected/What happened chart, then writes two sentences on the irony.

questions.q: What do the kidnappers expect, and what actually happens?
questions.a: They expect Ebenezer Dorset to pay $2,000 for his son; instead the boy torments them so much that they pay the father $250 to take him back.

days.guide: Reread a paragraph of Sam's narration aloud, noticing his big words. The child rewrites it in plain third person and compares.

questions.q: How does Sam's narration create humor?
questions.a: He uses fancy, formal vocabulary to describe a ridiculous, chaotic situation, and as the narrator he is clearly the one being outsmarted by a child.

days.guide: Read both stories once for fun, then reread to mark clues. Discuss which ending felt fair.

questions.q: In 'After Twenty Years', who is the patrolman, and why doesn't he make the arrest himself?
questions.a: He is Jimmy Wells. He recognizes Bob as a man wanted in Chicago and, not wanting to arrest his old friend himself, sends a plainclothes officer.

questions.q: In 'The Open Window', what is the twist?
questions.a: Vera made up the tragic story; the men return safely, Framton flees in terror, and Vera immediately invents another tale. 'Romance at short notice was her speciality.'

days.guide: Model: read the sentence, guess the meaning from clues, then check the dictionary. The child does 10 words from the stories.

questions.q: What clue types can help define a word?
questions.a: Definition/restatement, synonyms, antonyms or contrast, examples, and the general sense of the sentence.

days.guide: The child writes the comparison and takes the quiz.

questions.q: What kind of irony is the ending of 'The Ransom of Red Chief'?
questions.a: Situational irony — the kidnappers end up paying the victim's father.

weeks.assessment_key: Comparison paragraph (4 = names two stories, explains each point of view — e.g., Sam's first-person narration in 'Red Chief' hides nothing yet his pompous voice makes the reversal funny; the third-person narrator in 'After Twenty Years' withholds the patrolman's identity; 'The Open Window' lets us believe Vera's story along with Framton — and how it creates surprise, with evidence; 3 = accurate but thin; 2 = summary; 1 = incorrect). Quiz: 1) situational irony = outcome opposite of expectation 2) Red Chief irony: the father makes the kidnappers pay $250 to take the boy back 3) After Twenty Years: Jimmy Wells is the patrolman 4) The Open Window: Vera invented the tragedy 5–8) pronoun case items as in Week 1.

weeks.prep: Gather: mentor text: opening of 'Rikki-Tikki-Tavi', writing notebook. Model a heart map of your own to show the child.
misconceptions: Choosing a huge topic ('my summer vacation'). Narrow to one small moment lasting minutes.
Dialogue punctuation errors: commas and periods go inside quotation marks, and a new paragraph starts with each new speaker.

days.guide: Draw a heart map together; the child chooses one small moment and tells it aloud in two minutes while you time and ask one question.

questions.q: Is 'my trip to Yosemite' a small moment? How could it be narrowed?
questions.a: Too big. Narrow to one moment, e.g., the minute you reached the top of the trail and saw the waterfall.

days.guide: Show Kipling's first sentence ('This is the story of the great war that Rikki-tikki-tavi fought single-handed…') as a lead that hooks us. The child drafts three different leads.

questions.q: Name three types of leads and give an example of one.
questions.a: Action ('I slipped on the wet rock'), dialogue ('"Don't look down," Dad said'), setting ('The lake was silver and still').

days.guide: Review dialogue punctuation with one modeled line. The child drafts the middle with at least four lines.

questions.q: Punctuate: we're almost there said Mom
questions.a: "We're almost there," said Mom.

days.guide: Model slowing down a moment: what you saw, heard, felt, thought, second by second. The child expands their key moment.

questions.q: What can a writer add to slow down an important moment?
questions.a: Sensory details (sight, sound, touch, smell), inner thoughts and feelings, and small actions in sequence.

days.guide: The child drafts a reflective ending and reads the full draft aloud; give one 'glow' and one 'grow'.

questions.q: What should a reflective ending do?
questions.a: Show why the moment mattered or what the writer learned, not just 'then I went home'.

weeks.assessment_key: Draft checklist (check each): one focused moment; a lead that is action, dialogue or setting; clear sequence with transitions; at least four lines of correctly punctuated dialogue; one slowed-down moment of at least a paragraph with sensory details and thoughts; an ending that reflects on why it mattered. 6/6 = ready to revise; 4–5 = add missing elements; ≤3 = conference and redraft.

weeks.prep: Gather: narrative draft, computer for typing. Make sure a computer or tablet is available for typing on Day 4.
misconceptions: Revising means only fixing spelling. Revision changes ideas, words and sentences; editing fixes conventions.
Starting many sentences with 'I' or 'Then'. Try beginning with a time phrase, an action verb, or a describing word.

days.guide: Model rewriting three sentences that all start with 'I'. The child revises ten so no two in a row start the same way.

questions.q: Revise: 'I ran. I saw the dog. I yelled.'
questions.a: Example: 'Racing down the path, I spotted the dog and yelled.'

days.guide: Hunt for weak verbs (went, got, said) and vague nouns (stuff, thing); the child highlights five replacements.

questions.q: Give a stronger verb for 'went' in 'I went down the hill.'
questions.a: Sprinted, tumbled, crept, slid — depending on meaning.

days.guide: Use the checklist; the child edits, then you conference for 10 minutes on two things only.

questions.q: Which is correct: 'Dad and me laughed' or 'Dad and I laughed'?
questions.a: 'Dad and I laughed' (subject).

days.guide: The child types the final copy (2+ pages) with a title.

questions.q: What makes a good title for a narrative?
questions.a: A short phrase that hints at the moment or its meaning without giving away the ending.

days.guide: Hold author's chair; the child reads with expression and self-scores on the rubric; give the vocabulary quiz.

questions.q: What is foreshadowing?
questions.a: Hints or clues about what will happen later in a story.

weeks.assessment_key: Published narrative — 4-point rubric — 4: focused small moment, engaging lead, well-paced sequence, correctly punctuated dialogue, vivid sensory detail and a reflective ending, few errors; 3: all elements present but uneven detail or several errors; 2: summary-like, little dialogue or detail, errors interfere; 1: incomplete or off-task. Vocabulary quiz: definitions and use-in-sentence for unit words (lead, dialogue, irony, foreshadowing, point of view, climax, sensory detail).

weeks.prep: Gather: Hatchet by Gary Paulsen (library copy), map of Canada. Get Hatchet (library). Parent preview: Brian's parents are divorcing and he carries 'the Secret' (he saw his mother with another man); the pilot has a fatal heart attack during the flight. Discuss these calmly.
misconceptions: Thinking the hatchet is just a tool. Point out it is a gift from his mother — tied to his feelings about her and the Secret.
Using 'myself' as a subject or object ('Mom and myself went'). Intensive pronouns only emphasize a noun already in the sentence.

days.guide: Read chapter 1 aloud together, then trace a route from New York to northern Canada on the map. Ask what we know about Brian and the Secret.

questions.q: Where is Brian going and why?
questions.a: To visit his father in the north woods of Canada (where his father works in the oil fields) — his parents are divorced.

days.guide: Read chapters 2–3. The child lists sensory words and finds a run of short sentences, reading them aloud to feel the pace.

questions.q: Why does Paulsen use short sentences and fragments during the crash?
questions.a: They speed up the pace and copy Brian's panicked, choppy thoughts, building tension.

days.guide: Read chapter 4. The child makes a T-chart (physical: mosquitoes, hunger, injuries; emotional: fear, loneliness, the Secret).

questions.q: Which of Brian's problems is worse at first, physical or emotional? Use evidence.
questions.a: Accept either with evidence; e.g., emotional — memories of the Secret and fear overwhelm him and he cries, while physical problems like hunger and mosquitoes are painful but manageable.

days.guide: Teach that intensive pronouns emphasize ('Brian himself built the fire') and can be removed without changing meaning. The child writes 8 and fixes 6.

questions.q: Correct: 'The pilot and myself flew north.'
questions.a: 'The pilot and I flew north.'

questions.q: Write a sentence with an intensive pronoun about Brian.
questions.a: Example: 'Brian himself had to find food.'

days.guide: Give the reading check; the child writes a journal entry as Brian after the first night.

questions.q: What gift does Brian receive from his mother?
questions.a: A hatchet, worn on his belt.

weeks.assessment_key: Reading quiz (chapters 1–4): 1) Brian is 13 and flying in a small bush plane to visit his father in the Canadian north woods (oil fields) 2) His mother gave him a hatchet 3) The Secret: he saw his mother kissing a man who was not his father 4) The pilot has a heart attack 5) Brian crash-lands in a lake. Journal rubric: 4 = first-person voice, accurate events, physical and emotional details (mosquitoes, hunger, fear, memories of the Secret); 3 = accurate but less detail; 2 = errors; 1 = off-topic.

weeks.prep: Gather: Hatchet, ReadWorks or CommonLit wilderness survival article, National Park Service 'Ten Essentials' list. Print the National Park Service 'Ten Essentials' list and one survival article (ReadWorks/CommonLit). Preview: Brian gets sick from berries and is attacked by a porcupine.
misconceptions: Including opinions in an objective summary ('This awesome article…'). Summaries report only the central idea and key details.
Confusing personification with any description. Personification gives human qualities to non-human things ('the fire was a friend').

days.guide: Read chapters 5–6 (note page numbers). The child lists decisions and rates each smart or risky.

questions.q: Name one smart decision and one risky decision Brian makes early.
questions.a: Smart: building a shelter under the rock overhang near water. Risky: eating large amounts of the unknown 'gut cherries,' which make him sick.

days.guide: Read chapters 7–8. The child writes a paragraph on the self-pity lesson with two quotes.

questions.q: What does Brian learn after the porcupine attack?
questions.a: That feeling sorry for himself and crying doesn't change anything — self-pity didn't work, so he has to keep trying.

days.guide: Read chapter 9 and annotate how fire is described like a companion.

questions.q: How does Paulsen personify the fire?
questions.a: He calls it a friend and describes it as if it were alive and keeping Brian company and safe, giving it human qualities.

days.guide: Read the article and Ten Essentials list; model the first sentence of an objective summary.

questions.q: What does 'objective' mean in a summary?
questions.a: Neutral — only the text's ideas, no personal opinions or reactions.

days.guide: The child completes a Venn diagram and takes the quiz.

questions.q: Name one thing Brian lacks that is on the Ten Essentials list.
questions.a: Examples: a map/navigation, extra food, extra water, first aid kit, fire starter, sun protection, extra clothing, a light, emergency shelter.

weeks.assessment_key: Objective summary rubric: 4 = states the article's central idea in the first sentence, 3–4 key details in the author's order, no opinion, own words, 4–5 sentences; 3 = one opinion or a missing key detail; 2 = retelling or copying; 1 = off-topic. Reading quiz (ch. 5–9): 1) shelter under a rock overhang by the lake 2) 'gut cherries' make him sick; he finds raspberries 3) a bear at the raspberries leaves him alone 4) a porcupine attacks at night; quills in his leg 5) the hatchet striking rock makes sparks, leading to fire 6) lesson: self-pity doesn't work.

weeks.prep: Gather: Hatchet, character-change chart. Parent preview (important): after the rescue plane passes without seeing him, Brian sinks into despair and attempts to take his own life before deciding to keep living (the 'new Brian'). Read this section first and be ready to talk about it; reassure your child and share where help is available (988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline).
misconceptions: Stating a theme as one word ('survival'). A theme is a full sentence about life: 'Hope and patience help people survive hardship.'
Pronoun shifts ('If a person gets lost, you should…'). Keep the same person/number throughout.

days.guide: Read chapters 10–11. The child records each failure and what Brian learns.

questions.q: What does 'tough hope' mean?
questions.a: Hope that is realistic and lasting — based on Brian's own skill and effort rather than wishing for rescue.

days.guide: Read chapter 12. Discuss the turning point gently; the child writes a journal entry analyzing it.

questions.q: Why is the missed rescue plane a turning point?
questions.a: Brian's hope of quick rescue is crushed; after his lowest moment he decides to survive on his own and becomes tougher and more determined.

days.guide: Read chapter 13. The child completes a then/now chart with evidence.

questions.q: Give one difference between Brian at the start and the 'new Brian.'
questions.a: Then: panicked and helpless. Now: observant and patient, learning from mistakes, hunting with a bow and getting food on his own.

days.guide: Teach pronoun shifts; the child corrects 12 sentences.

questions.q: Correct: 'If a person gets lost, you should stay calm.'
questions.a: 'If a person gets lost, he or she should stay calm.' or 'If you get lost, you should stay calm.'

days.guide: The child drafts a theme statement with three details and takes the quiz.

questions.q: Write a theme for Hatchet in one sentence.
questions.a: Example: 'Patience and learning from mistakes help people survive hardship.'

weeks.assessment_key: Theme paragraph rubric: 4 = full-sentence theme (e.g., 'Learning from mistakes and holding on to hope can help a person survive'), three accurate supporting details (foolbird hunting failures, making a bow and fish spear, the 'tough hope' after the plane passes), explained; 3 = theme plus two details; 2 = topic word only; 1 = no support. Quiz (ch. 10–13): 1) foolbirds are hard to see because of camouflage; he learns to look for shapes 2) he makes a fish spear and later a bow 3) a search plane passes without seeing him 4) after despair, Brian becomes the 'new Brian' who has tough hope 5) he learns that mistakes are teachers.

weeks.prep: Gather: Hatchet, library audiobook of Hatchet (optional). Optional audiobook from the library app. Preview: Brian sees the pilot's remains when he returns to the plane (brief).
misconceptions: Thinking the epilogue is unimportant. It reveals how long he survived and how the experience changed him.
Assuming the narrator's voice must match their own mental voice; compare thoughtfully.

days.guide: Read chapters 14–15. Ask how Brian responds to setbacks now compared with earlier.

questions.q: How does the 'new Brian' respond after the tornado destroys his camp?
questions.a: He doesn't give up; he starts rebuilding and decides to go after the survival pack in the plane.

days.guide: Read chapters 16–17; the child lists survival-pack items and predicts.

questions.q: Why does Brian want to reach the plane?
questions.a: To get the survival pack — it might contain food and supplies to help him last.

days.guide: Read chapters 18–19 and the epilogue; discuss the transmitter.

questions.q: How is Brian rescued?
questions.a: He unknowingly switches on the emergency transmitter from the survival pack, and a pilot hears the signal and lands on the lake.

days.guide: Listen to one chapter while following along; note the narrator's choices.

questions.q: What can a narrator's voice add to a book?
questions.a: Mood and pacing through tone, pauses and emphasis; it can make tense scenes more intense or change how a character sounds to us.

days.guide: Give the test independently.

questions.q: How long was Brian in the wilderness?
questions.a: 54 days.

weeks.assessment_key: Hatchet test key: 1) a moose attacks him in the lake 2) a tornado wrecks his camp and lifts the plane's tail 3) he retrieves the survival pack from the plane 4) the pack contains an emergency transmitter, which he turns on without realizing it 5) a pilot answering the signal rescues him 6) Brian survived 54 days. Short responses (4 = claim + two text details + explanation): how Brian changes; why the epilogue matters (shows lasting changes, e.g., he is more observant and thinks before acting, and notes that if not rescued he would have faced winter).

weeks.prep: Gather: Hatchet notes, survival article, essay organizer. Gather Hatchet notes and the Week 6 survival article; print an essay organizer.
misconceptions: Retelling the plot in body paragraphs. Each paragraph needs a topic sentence, evidence and explanation of how it shows survival.
Citing the article without naming it. Teach 'According to…'.

days.guide: Model a thesis: 'Brian survives because he masters fire, learns to find food and develops tough hope.' The child writes theirs and fills the organizer.

questions.q: What makes a thesis strong?
questions.a: It answers the prompt directly and previews the main points.

days.guide: The child drafts three body paragraphs with a Hatchet quote and an article fact in each.

questions.q: What should come right after a quotation?
questions.a: Explanation of how it supports the paragraph's point.

days.guide: Discuss hooks (question, surprising fact, quote). The child drafts intro and conclusion.

questions.q: What should the conclusion do?
questions.a: Restate the thesis in new words and explain what Brian's survival teaches readers.

days.guide: Revise for transitions; edit for pronoun shifts and intensive pronouns; type final.

questions.q: Name three transitions for explanatory writing.
questions.a: First, in addition, for example, finally, as a result.

days.guide: Child submits, self-scores and takes the vocabulary test.

questions.q: Define 'epilogue.'
questions.a: A section after the main story that tells what happened later.

weeks.assessment_key: Explanatory essay rubric — 4: clear thesis naming three ways Brian survives (e.g., making fire, finding food, keeping a positive mental attitude/'tough hope'); each body paragraph has a quote from Hatchet and a fact from the article, explained; hook intro and meaningful conclusion; transitions; few errors. 3: all parts but some evidence unexplained. 2: missing evidence or a paragraph. 1: incomplete. Vocabulary test covers unit words (theme, personification, objective summary, intensive pronoun, epilogue, turning point).

weeks.prep: Gather: 'A Wonder-Book' and 'Tanglewood Tales' by Nathaniel Hawthorne (Project Gutenberg), D'Aulaires' Book of Greek Myths (library, optional). Download A Wonder-Book (Pandora: 'The Paradise of Children'; Midas: 'The Golden Touch'). Prometheus is in D'Aulaires' or any myth collection.
misconceptions: Thinking myths are just 'made-up stories'. Myths explained nature and taught values to ancient people.
Guessing meaning from one root without checking. Verify with a dictionary.

days.guide: Read the Prometheus myth. The child lists what it explains and discusses why cultures made myths.

questions.q: What does the Prometheus myth explain?
questions.a: How humans got fire (Prometheus stole it from the gods); in many versions it also explains human suffering because Zeus punishes humans and Prometheus.

days.guide: Read 'The Paradise of Children'. The child writes the theme with evidence.

questions.q: What remains in the box after the Troubles escape, and why does it matter?
questions.a: Hope; it suggests that hope helps people bear life's troubles.

days.guide: Read 'The Golden Touch'. Trace Midas's choices from wish to loss to resolution.

questions.q: How does Midas's golden touch become a curse?
questions.a: His food turns to gold so he can't eat, and he turns his beloved daughter Marygold into a gold statue.

days.guide: Build a root map from the myth words.

questions.q: Where does 'panic' come from?
questions.a: From Pan, the god said to cause sudden fear in people.

days.guide: Give the quiz; the child retells a myth orally.

questions.q: What is a theme of the Midas story?
questions.a: Greed can destroy what truly matters; love is worth more than wealth.

weeks.assessment_key: Roots quiz sample: 1) chron = time (chronology) 2) psych = mind/soul 3) narcissist = person too absorbed in himself (Narcissus) 4) echo (the nymph Echo) 5) panic (Pan) 6) tantalize = tease with something out of reach (Tantalus) 7) graph = write 8) tele = far 9) bio = life 10) phon = sound. Oral retelling rubric: 4 = correct sequence, main characters, the explanation/lesson, clear voice under 2 minutes; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = confused order; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather: 'The Children's Homer' by Padraic Colum (Project Gutenberg), map of the Mediterranean. Download The Children's Homer (Colum) and print a Mediterranean map. Preview: the Cyclops episode includes the giant eating crew members.
misconceptions: Thinking an epic hero is perfect. Odysseus is brave and clever but also proud and boastful.
Assuming the crew's problems are only bad luck. Choices (opening the winds bag, taunting the Cyclops) cause them.

days.guide: Read the opening; map Troy to Ithaca. The child lists epic-hero traits.

questions.q: What is Odysseus trying to do?
questions.a: Return home to Ithaca after the Trojan War, to his wife Penelope and son Telemachus.

days.guide: Read the Cyclops episode; the child cites evidence for clever and proud.

questions.q: Give evidence Odysseus is clever and proud in the Cyclops episode.
questions.a: Clever: he calls himself 'Noman' and escapes by hiding his men under the rams. Proud: he shouts his real name as they sail away, so Polyphemus can ask Poseidon for revenge.

days.guide: Read the Aeolus and Circe episodes; chart choice → consequence.

questions.q: What happens when the crew opens the bag of winds?
questions.a: The winds burst out and blow the ships away from Ithaca, just when home was in sight.

days.guide: The child finds 10 words with Greek/Latin parts and analyzes them.

questions.q: Analyze 'monstrous.'
questions.a: Monster + -ous (full of/having the qualities of): like a monster.

days.guide: The child writes the analytical paragraph and takes the quiz.

questions.q: Why is Poseidon angry with Odysseus?
questions.a: Odysseus blinded Poseidon's son Polyphemus.

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric: 4 = names a flaw (usually pride/hubris), chooses an episode (e.g., shouting his real name to Polyphemus, which brings Poseidon's anger) with evidence and explanation; 3 = adequate; 2 = retelling; 1 = off-topic. Reading quiz: 1) Odysseus fought at Troy and is trying to get home to Ithaca 2) he tells the Cyclops his name is 'Noman' 3) blinds Polyphemus with a sharpened stake 4) the men escape clinging under the rams 5) Aeolus gives a bag of winds that the crew opens near Ithaca 6) Circe turns the men into swine.

weeks.prep: Gather: The Children's Homer, audio or animated clip of the Sirens episode. Find a short audio or animated retelling of the Sirens episode (preview for scariness).
misconceptions: Writing a theme as a topic ('loyalty'). Make it a statement: 'True loyalty endures through long separation.'
Assuming a film version is 'the same story'. List specifically what was added, cut or changed.

days.guide: Read Sirens and Scylla. Discuss temptation and the hard choices of a leader.

questions.q: How does Odysseus get past the Sirens?
questions.a: He plugs the crew's ears with wax and has himself tied to the mast so he can hear but not steer toward them.

days.guide: Read the return to Ithaca and Penelope's test.

questions.q: How does Penelope test Odysseus?
questions.a: She orders the bed moved; he angrily says it can't be, since he built it around a living olive tree — a secret only he would know.

days.guide: The child writes two theme statements with evidence.

questions.q: Write a theme about loyalty in the Odyssey.
questions.a: Example: 'True loyalty lasts through long hardship' — Penelope waits twenty years and refuses the suitors.

days.guide: Watch/listen to the retelling; complete the added/cut/changed chart.

questions.q: Why might a film add or change details?
questions.a: To make it more visual or dramatic, fit time limits or suit its audience.

days.guide: The child writes the comparison and takes the quiz.

questions.q: What is Charybdis?
questions.a: A whirlpool that swallows the sea.

weeks.assessment_key: Comparison rubric: 4 = explains how both texts treat pride (e.g., Midas's pride/greed or Arachne's boasting is punished; Odysseus's boasting to the Cyclops prolongs his journey) with evidence from each and a shared theme; 3 = both texts discussed but thin; 2 = one text; 1 = off-topic. Quiz: 1) crew's ears stopped with wax; Odysseus tied to the mast 2) Scylla is a six-headed monster, Charybdis a whirlpool 3) Odysseus returns disguised as a beggar 4) he strings the great bow and shoots through the axes 5) Penelope tests him about their bed, which he built from a living olive tree, so it cannot be moved.

weeks.prep: Gather: hero's journey diagram, computer. Print a hero's journey diagram (ordinary world, call to adventure, trials, climax, return).
misconceptions: Making the story all action with no character change. A hero's journey shows the hero changing.
Shifting tense (past to present) mid-story. Choose one tense and keep it.

days.guide: Map Odysseus and Brian onto the hero's journey together; the child plans their own.

questions.q: Map Brian onto two stages of the hero's journey.
questions.a: Call to adventure: the plane crash; trials: hunger, the porcupine, the moose and tornado; return: rescue, changed.

days.guide: The child drafts the opening and call to adventure with vivid setting.

questions.q: What is a call to adventure?
questions.a: The event that pulls the hero out of ordinary life into the challenge.

days.guide: The child drafts two trials with dialogue and time-shift transitions.

questions.q: Give three transitions showing time shifts.
questions.a: Later that night; three days passed; meanwhile.

days.guide: Revise the climax and return; edit for pronoun case and verb tense; type final.

questions.q: Correct the tense shift: 'She ran to the cave and grabs the torch.'
questions.a: 'She ran to the cave and grabbed the torch.'

days.guide: The child reads aloud, self-scores, and takes the unit test.

questions.q: What is hubris?
questions.a: Excessive pride, which often leads to a hero's downfall in Greek stories.

weeks.assessment_key: Narrative 4-point rubric — 4: focused small moment, engaging lead, well-paced sequence, correctly punctuated dialogue, vivid sensory detail and a reflective ending, few errors; 3: all elements present but uneven detail or several errors; 2: summary-like, little dialogue or detail, errors interfere; 1: incomplete or off-task. Unit test sample: 1) myth = traditional story explaining nature or teaching values 2) epic hero = larger-than-life hero on a long journey 3) Prometheus stole fire for humans 4) Pandora's box left Hope 5) Polyphemus is a Cyclops, son of Poseidon 6) Odysseus's flaw = pride 7) hubris = excessive pride.

weeks.prep: Gather: CommonLit argument articles (e.g., on school start times, homework, screen time), highlighters. Choose two CommonLit argument articles (e.g., later school start times) and print them; get three highlighter colors.
misconceptions: Treating an opinion as an argument. An argument has a claim supported by reasons and evidence.
Accepting any evidence. Ask: Is it relevant? Is there enough? Is it from a reliable source?

days.guide: Show 'Pizza is food' (fact), 'Pizza is delicious' (opinion), and a claim with reasons. The child finds claims in 6 ads/excerpts.

questions.q: Is 'Schools should start at 8:30 because teens need more sleep' a fact, opinion or argument?
questions.a: An argument — a claim supported by a reason.

days.guide: Model annotating claim (one color), reasons (second), evidence (third).

questions.q: What is the difference between a reason and evidence?
questions.a: A reason explains why the claim is true; evidence (facts, data, expert quotes) proves the reason.

days.guide: The child labels each piece of evidence relevant, sufficient or unsupported.

questions.q: Evidence: 'My cousin is always tired in the morning.' Is it sufficient to prove all teens need later starts?
questions.a: No — one person's experience is not enough evidence for a general claim.

days.guide: Find loaded words (e.g., 'cruel', 'ridiculous') and discuss point of view.

questions.q: What are loaded words?
questions.a: Words with strong emotional connotations that push the reader toward the author's view.

days.guide: The child analyzes a new argument independently.

questions.q: What should you identify first when analyzing an argument?
questions.a: The author's claim (main position).

weeks.assessment_key: Argument-analysis organizer key (for any short article): Claim — one sentence of the author's position; Reasons — 2–3; Evidence — the facts, statistics, or expert quotes for each; evaluation — whether evidence is relevant and sufficient; Point of view and any loaded words. 4 = all parts accurate; 3 = one part weak; 2 = claim or reasons misidentified; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather: two to three articles on a chosen issue (e.g., Should zoos exist? Should kids have phones?), note cards. Choose 2–3 balanced articles on one issue the child cares about.
misconceptions: Choosing a non-debatable topic ('Dogs are animals'). The question must have reasonable sides.
Vague pronouns: 'they say' or 'this' with no clear noun. Replace with the specific noun.

days.guide: The child chooses a question, reads two articles and takes a position.

questions.q: Is 'Should kids have phones?' debatable? Why?
questions.a: Yes — reasonable people disagree and evidence exists on both sides.

days.guide: Model a quote card and a paraphrase card with source title.

questions.q: What is the difference between a quotation and a paraphrase?
questions.a: A quotation uses the author's exact words in quotation marks; a paraphrase restates the idea in your own words (still cited).

days.guide: Teach vague pronouns; the child fixes 12.

questions.q: Fix: 'When Sam called Leo, he was upset.'
questions.a: Name who was upset: 'Leo was upset when Sam called him.'

days.guide: The child completes the outline including counterclaim and rebuttal.

questions.q: What is a rebuttal?
questions.a: Your response showing why the opposing claim is weaker or wrong.

days.guide: The child explains the outline orally; ask questions; give the quiz.

questions.q: Fix: 'This is why we should go.'
questions.a: Replace 'this' with a specific noun phrase, e.g., 'The cheaper ticket price is why we should go.'

weeks.assessment_key: Outline check: claim; 2–3 reasons; evidence (with source) for each; a counterclaim; rebuttal. 4 = complete and logical; 3 = one weak area; 2 = missing counterclaim or evidence; 1 = incomplete. Vague pronoun quiz sample answers: 'They say phones distract' → 'Researchers at ___ found…'; 'This is a problem' → 'This lack of sleep is a problem'; 'Mom told Aunt Jo that she was late' → 'Mom told Aunt Jo, "I am late."'

weeks.prep: Gather: outline, computer. Have the outline and a computer ready.
misconceptions: Writing 'I think' or 'In my opinion'. State the claim directly.
Dropping evidence in without explaining how it supports the reason.

days.guide: Model a hook, two background sentences and a precise claim.

questions.q: Make this claim more precise: 'Phones are bad.'
questions.a: Example: 'Middle schools should require students to keep phones in lockers during class because phones distract from learning.'

days.guide: The child drafts body paragraphs; check each has evidence + explanation.

questions.q: What sentence frame helps explain evidence?
questions.a: 'This shows that… because…'

days.guide: The child drafts counterclaim/rebuttal and conclusion.

questions.q: Give a frame for a counterclaim.
questions.a: 'Some people argue that… However, …'

days.guide: Revise for formal tone and transitions.

questions.q: Rewrite formally: 'Homework is super dumb.'
questions.a: Example: 'Excessive homework provides little benefit for students.'

days.guide: Edit, type, self-score.

questions.q: Name two transitions that show contrast.
questions.a: However; on the other hand; although.

weeks.assessment_key: Argument essay rubric — 4: precise claim; 2–3 reasons, each with relevant evidence and explanation; counterclaim fairly stated and rebutted; formal style; transitions; conclusion follows from the argument; few errors. 3: all parts, some explanation thin. 2: missing counterclaim or weak evidence. 1: incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather: essay, timer, a recorded student speech or TED-Ed talk. Choose a short persuasive speech (a TED-Ed or student speech; preview it). Arrange a debate partner.
misconceptions: Reading the speech word-for-word. Use note cards with key words only.
Ignoring the opponent's points in rebuttal. Listen and respond to specific claims.

days.guide: Watch the speech; the child notes claims and support.

questions.q: How can you tell if a speaker's claim is supported?
questions.a: They give evidence such as facts, data, examples or expert statements that relate directly to the claim.

days.guide: The child turns the essay into a 2-minute statement on cards.

questions.q: What goes on a note card?
questions.a: Key words and phrases, not full sentences.

days.guide: Record practice; the child critiques eye contact, volume and pace.

questions.q: Name two delivery skills to check on the video.
questions.a: Eye contact, volume, pace, gestures, clear pronunciation.

days.guide: Hold the debate: openings (2 min), rebuttals (1 min), closings (1 min).

questions.q: What makes a good rebuttal?
questions.a: It restates the opponent's point fairly and answers it with reasoning or evidence.

days.guide: The child reflects and takes the unit test.

questions.q: Define counterclaim.
questions.a: An opposing position to your claim.

weeks.assessment_key: Debate rubric (4/3/2/1): claim clarity; evidence; rebuttal responds directly to opponent's points; delivery (eye contact, volume, pace); respectful conduct. Unit test sample: claim = position; reason; evidence; counterclaim; rebuttal; relevant vs. sufficient evidence; loaded words; formal style.

weeks.prep: Gather: 'Fog' by Carl Sandburg, 'Hope is the thing with feathers' by Emily Dickinson, 'Dreams' by Langston Hughes. Print 'Fog', 'Hope is the thing with feathers', 'Dreams' and 'Mother to Son' (Poetry Foundation or library).
misconceptions: Confusing simile and metaphor. A simile uses like/as; a metaphor says one thing is another.
Thinking connotation is the dictionary meaning. Connotation is the feeling a word carries.

days.guide: Read 'Fog' twice; the child sketches the image and explains the metaphor.

questions.q: What is fog compared to in 'Fog', and what does that suggest?
questions.a: A cat — it arrives silently ('little cat feet'), sits watching the harbor and city 'on silent haunches,' and then moves on, suggesting fog is quiet and changeable.

days.guide: Read Dickinson's poem; annotate stanza by stanza.

questions.q: How does Dickinson develop the bird metaphor?
questions.a: Hope perches in the soul and sings without words and never stops; it sings sweetest in the storm and keeps many warm; and it never asks 'a crumb' in return.

days.guide: Read 'Dreams' and 'Mother to Son'; compare metaphors and tones.

questions.q: Compare the metaphors in 'Dreams' and 'Mother to Son.'
questions.a: 'Dreams' compares life without dreams to a broken-winged bird and a barren, frozen field (urgent, warning tone); 'Mother to Son' compares life to a stair that 'ain't been no crystal stair' with tacks and splinters (determined, encouraging tone: keep climbing).

days.guide: Sort connotation pairs; the child rewrites a stanza changing tone.

questions.q: Which word has a more positive connotation: thrifty or stingy?
questions.a: Thrifty (careful with money); stingy suggests selfishness.

days.guide: The child writes an extended-metaphor poem and takes the quiz.

questions.q: What is an extended metaphor?
questions.a: A metaphor carried through several lines or a whole poem.

weeks.assessment_key: Figurative-language quiz sample: 1) 'The fog comes on little cat feet' — metaphor (fog as a cat) 2) 'Hope is the thing with feathers' — metaphor (hope as a bird) 3) 'Life for me ain't been no crystal stair' — metaphor 4) 'as busy as a bee' — simile 5) 'the wind whispered' — personification 6) 'I've told you a million times' — hyperbole. Poem rubric: 4 = one metaphor developed across the poem, vivid images, deliberate line breaks; 3 = metaphor not fully extended; 2 = scattered images; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather: 'Paul Revere's Ride' by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, 'The Raven' (excerpt) by Edgar Allan Poe, audio recordings. Print 'Paul Revere's Ride' and the first stanzas of 'The Raven'; find a professional recording (LibriVox or Poetry Foundation).
misconceptions: Thinking every poem rhymes in couplets. Label rhyme with letters to see each pattern.
Mixing up alliteration (repeated beginning consonant sounds) and internal rhyme (rhyme inside a line).

days.guide: Read 'Paul Revere's Ride' aloud while the child taps the beat on the table. Ask what the rhythm sounds like.

questions.q: How does the rhythm of 'Paul Revere's Ride' match its content?
questions.a: Its quick, galloping beat imitates the hoofbeats of Revere's horse racing through the night, building urgency.

days.guide: Model labeling rhyme with letters; the child labels three poems and marks sound devices in 'The Raven'.

questions.q: Find alliteration and internal rhyme in 'Once upon a midnight dreary, while I pondered, weak and weary… While I nodded, nearly napping, suddenly there came a tapping.'
questions.a: Internal rhyme: dreary/weary, napping/tapping. Alliteration: nodded, nearly, napping.

days.guide: Read the Raven excerpt silently, then listen to a recording. Compare.

questions.q: What does hearing a professional reading add?
questions.a: Tone of voice, pacing and pauses create a gloomy, eerie mood and make the rhythm and repeated sounds stand out.

days.guide: Choose the lantern/belfry stanza; discuss how it fits the whole poem's suspense.

questions.q: What is the signal in 'Paul Revere's Ride', and why does waiting for it build suspense?
questions.a: Lanterns in the Old North Church tower: 'One, if by land, and two, if by sea.' Revere — and the reader — wait to see the light, delaying the action.

days.guide: The child recites 12+ lines and takes the quiz.

questions.q: What is a refrain?
questions.a: A repeated line or word, like 'Nevermore' in 'The Raven'.

weeks.assessment_key: Sound-device quiz: 1) 'while I nodded, nearly napping' — alliteration 2) 'dreary / weary' in one line — internal rhyme 3) 'Nevermore' repeated — refrain/repetition 4) the galloping rhythm of 'Paul Revere's Ride' imitates a horse's hooves 5) rhyme scheme: label a given stanza with letters (e.g., Raven stanza ABCBBB). Recitation rubric: 4 = 12+ lines memorized, expressive pacing, clear volume, eye contact; 3 = minor prompts; 2 = several prompts or flat delivery; 1 = read from paper.

weeks.prep: Gather: 'The Road Not Taken' by Robert Frost, 'Who Has Seen the Wind?' by Christina Rossetti, 'The Land of Counterpane' by Robert Louis Stevenson. Print 'The Road Not Taken', 'Who Has Seen the Wind?' and 'The Land of Counterpane'; choose a free-verse poem from CommonLit.
misconceptions: Assuming the poet and speaker are the same person. The speaker is the voice in the poem.
Reading 'The Road Not Taken' as simply 'be a nonconformist'. The speaker admits the roads were 'really about the same'.

days.guide: Read the Frost poem twice. Ask who is speaking and what situation they're in.

questions.q: Describe the speaker's situation in 'The Road Not Taken'.
questions.a: Standing in a yellow wood where two roads split, the speaker must choose one and knows he probably won't come back to try the other.

days.guide: Point out lines saying the roads were 'worn… really about the same'; debate the theme. The child writes a theme paragraph.

questions.q: Is the poem really about choosing the 'less traveled' road? Use evidence.
questions.a: Not simply: the speaker says the roads were worn 'really about the same,' and predicts he will tell the story 'with a sigh' 'ages and ages hence.' A theme: people later give their choices meaning when telling their life stories.

days.guide: Read Rossetti and Stevenson; choose tone words with line evidence.

questions.q: Give a tone word for 'Who Has Seen the Wind?' and evidence.
questions.a: Gentle/wondering: we can't see the wind, but 'when the leaves hang trembling, / The wind is passing through.'

questions.q: Give a tone word for 'The Land of Counterpane'.
questions.a: Cheerful/imaginative: a sick child plays on the bedclothes as 'the giant great and still / That sits upon the pillow-hill.'

days.guide: Compare a free-verse poem's structure with Frost's rhymed five-line stanzas.

questions.q: What is the rhyme scheme of each stanza of 'The Road Not Taken'?
questions.a: ABAAB, in four five-line stanzas.

days.guide: The child analyzes an unseen poem independently.

questions.q: What is the speaker of a poem?
questions.a: The voice telling the poem, which may not be the poet.

weeks.assessment_key: Independent analysis rubric (any unseen poem): 4 = identifies speaker and situation, names precise tone words with lines that create them, states a theme as a sentence with evidence; 3 = two of three strong; 2 = mostly summary; 1 = off-topic.

weeks.prep: Gather: notebook, art supplies, computer. Gather art supplies and a folder or binder for the anthology.
misconceptions: Haiku must be 5-7-5 and nothing else. Also emphasize nature focus and a fresh image.
Forcing rhymes that make no sense. Meaning comes first.

days.guide: Read an ode example (e.g., Pablo Neruda's 'Ode to My Socks' or a CommonLit ode). The child writes an ode to an ordinary object.

questions.q: What is an ode?
questions.a: A poem praising or celebrating a person, object or idea, often with strong feeling.

days.guide: Review haiku form; the child writes three from outdoor observation and one concrete poem.

questions.q: What is the syllable pattern of a traditional English haiku?
questions.a: 5-7-5 syllables in three lines.

days.guide: Reread a Longfellow stanza for model; the child writes a narrative poem with a rhyme scheme.

questions.q: What makes a poem a narrative poem?
questions.a: It tells a story with characters, events and a plot.

days.guide: The child revises and compiles 6–8 poems.

questions.q: What does an author's note include?
questions.a: Why the poet wrote the poems, inspirations and choices they made.

days.guide: Host the poetry café; give the unit test.

questions.q: What is free verse?
questions.a: Poetry without a regular rhyme scheme or meter.

weeks.assessment_key: Anthology rubric — 4: 6–8 polished poems (ode, haiku, concrete, narrative, plus choices), varied figurative language, table of contents, author's note, illustrations; 3: complete with less polish; 2: fewer than 6 poems or missing parts; 1: incomplete. Unit test sample: metaphor, simile, personification, alliteration, rhyme scheme, meter/rhythm, speaker, tone, theme, free verse, ode, haiku, extended metaphor, connotation.

weeks.prep: Gather: 'The Story of My Life' by Helen Keller (Project Gutenberg). Download 'The Story of My Life' (Project Gutenberg). Read chapters 1–4 yourself.
misconceptions: Thinking Helen was born blind and deaf. She lost sight and hearing from an illness at about 19 months.
Using commas for every interruption. Dashes add emphasis; parentheses play information down; commas are neutral.

days.guide: Read chapters 1–2. The child lists how Keller describes her illness and frustration, noting the adult looking back.

questions.q: How did Helen lose her sight and hearing?
questions.a: An illness when she was about 19 months old left her blind and deaf.

days.guide: Read chapters 3–4. Reread the well-house passage aloud; analyze word choice.

questions.q: How does Keller's language show the water moment was life-changing?
questions.a: She says 'That living word awakened my soul, gave it light, hope, joy, set it free!' — words of light and freedom show language opened her mind.

days.guide: Teach nonrestrictive elements and the three punctuation choices. The child punctuates 15 sentences.

questions.q: Punctuate three ways: Anne Sullivan her teacher arrived in 1887.
questions.a: 'Anne Sullivan, her teacher, arrived…'; 'Anne Sullivan (her teacher) arrived…'; 'Anne Sullivan—her teacher—arrived…'

days.guide: The child writes a paragraph on Keller's purpose with two quotations.

questions.q: Why might Keller have written her autobiography?
questions.a: To show others how language and education changed her life and to honor her teacher; to help people understand the experience of being deaf and blind.

days.guide: Give the reading and punctuation quizzes.

questions.q: Who was Anne Sullivan?
questions.a: Helen's teacher from the Perkins Institution, who arrived in 1887 and taught her language through finger-spelling.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) born in Tuscumbia, Alabama (1880) 2) an illness at 19 months left her blind and deaf 3) Anne Sullivan arrives March 3, 1887 — 'the most important day I remember in all my life' 4) the doll and the mug/water confusion 5) at the well-house, water poured over one hand while Sullivan spelled 'w-a-t-e-r' in the other. Punctuation: 'Anne Sullivan, her teacher, arrived in 1887.' / '…(her teacher)…' / '—her teacher—'. Purpose paragraph rubric: 4 = states a purpose (e.g., to share how language opened her world) with two quotes explained; 3 = one quote; 2 = summary; 1 = off-topic.

weeks.prep: Gather: The Story of My Life, Braille alphabet chart. Print a Braille alphabet chart; gather glue (dots) and cardstock.
misconceptions: Thinking an objective summary includes your reaction. Keep it neutral.
Thinking learning to speak was easy once Helen could spell. Chapter 13 shows it took enormous persistence.

days.guide: Read chapters 5–7; list Sullivan's methods.

questions.q: Name two methods Anne Sullivan used.
questions.a: Spelling words into Helen's hand connected to real objects; teaching outdoors through nature; letting her learn through experience and conversation rather than drills.

days.guide: Read about reading and writing; the child writes their name in Braille with glue dots.

questions.q: How many dots are in a Braille cell?
questions.a: Six (two columns of three).

days.guide: Read chapter 13; explain how it develops the central idea.

questions.q: How does learning to speak contribute to the central idea?
questions.a: It shows her determination and that communication kept expanding her world; she worked hard with a teacher (Sarah Fuller) to speak aloud.

days.guide: The child writes a 150-word objective summary.

questions.q: What should an objective summary's first sentence do?
questions.a: State the title, author and central idea.

days.guide: Give the quiz; discuss what surprised the child.

questions.q: What text structure does Keller mainly use?
questions.a: Chronological order (time order), with reflection from her adult point of view.

weeks.assessment_key: Objective summary rubric (150 words): 4 = central idea (language and a devoted teacher transformed Keller's life), key events in order (water, learning words, reading/Braille, learning to speak), neutral, own words; 3 = minor omission; 2 = opinion or copying; 1 = off-topic. Quiz: central idea = learning language opened Keller's world; structure = chronological autobiography with adult reflection; Sullivan spelled words into her hand, taught outdoors from nature, and connected words to experiences.

weeks.prep: Gather: a children's biography of Helen Keller (library), film clip of the water-pump scene from 'The Miracle Worker' (1962). Borrow a children's biography of Helen Keller; find the water-pump scene from 'The Miracle Worker' (1962; preview, it's intense but appropriate).
misconceptions: Thinking all versions are equally accurate. A memoir is a first-hand account; a biography is second-hand; a film dramatizes.
Listing differences without explaining why authors made those choices.

days.guide: Read the biography's account; annotate differences from Keller's.

questions.q: What can a biography include that a memoir might not?
questions.a: Outside perspectives, historical context, facts the subject didn't know or chose to leave out.

days.guide: Complete a chart: included, omitted, emphasized and why.

questions.q: Why does Keller's own account focus on feelings?
questions.a: As the person who lived it, she can describe her inner experience — her mind 'awakening'.

days.guide: Watch the scene; note acting, sound and camera.

questions.q: How does the film change the experience of the water scene?
questions.a: Actors, close-ups, sound of water and music make it dramatic and emotional to watch; we see it from outside rather than inside Helen's mind.

days.guide: Browse Library of Congress photos/letters of Keller.

questions.q: What does a primary source add?
questions.a: Direct evidence from the time — her real handwriting or photos — that makes her life more concrete.

days.guide: The child writes the comparison.

questions.q: Define memoir.
questions.a: A true account written by a person about their own experiences.

weeks.assessment_key: 3-paragraph comparison rubric — 4: compares Keller's first-person memoir (inner feelings, 'awakened my soul'), a biography (outside view, often adds context and others' observations), and the film (actors, sound, emotion, dramatic struggle at the pump); explains reasons for differences with evidence; 3: compares two well; 2: lists without explanation; 1: incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather: notebook, computer. Have the child think ahead about something hard they learned (riding a bike, a skill, a challenge).
misconceptions: Writing only events without reflection. Keller mixes narration with what it meant.
Overusing dashes; vary with commas and parentheses.

days.guide: Brainstorm learning moments; the child picks one and plans a turning point.

questions.q: What is a turning point in a memoir?
questions.a: The moment the writer's understanding or situation changes.

days.guide: The child drafts, mixing events with reflection.

questions.q: Write a reflection sentence like Keller's.
questions.a: Example: 'Looking back, I realize that falling was what finally taught me balance.'

days.guide: Revise for voice; add three nonrestrictive elements.

questions.q: Punctuate: My coach a patient man never yelled.
questions.a: 'My coach, a patient man, never yelled.' (or parentheses/dashes)

days.guide: Edit and type the chapter.

questions.q: Is a nonrestrictive element needed to identify the noun?
questions.a: No — it adds extra information and can be removed without changing the core meaning.

days.guide: The child reads aloud and takes the unit test.

questions.q: Primary or secondary source: Keller's autobiography?
questions.a: Primary source.

weeks.assessment_key: Memoir chapter rubric — 4: clear turning point, vivid narration, adult-like reflection on meaning, at least three correctly punctuated nonrestrictive elements, few errors; 3: reflection thin or punctuation inconsistent; 2: list of events; 1: incomplete. Unit test sample: central idea, objective summary, text structure, point of view/purpose, memoir vs. biography, primary vs. secondary source, nonrestrictive elements.

weeks.prep: Gather: 'Tales from Shakespeare' by Charles and Mary Lamb (Project Gutenberg), Folger Shakespeare text of A Midsummer Night's Dream (free online). Bookmark the Folger text of A Midsummer Night's Dream and the Lambs' retelling. Watch a short Globe Theatre video.
misconceptions: Assuming 'thou/thee' is fancy talk. It was informal 'you' in Shakespeare's time.
Confusing the four lovers. Keep a chart: Hermia ♥ Lysander; Demetrius wants Hermia; Helena ♥ Demetrius.

days.guide: Show pictures of the Globe (open-air, groundlings, no sets, men played women's roles). Read the Lambs' retelling for an overview.

questions.q: Name two features of the Globe Theatre.
questions.a: Open-air round theater; standing 'groundlings' near the stage; little scenery; all-male actors.

days.guide: Read Act 1 Scene 1 with glosses; chart the lovers.

questions.q: What is Hermia's conflict in Act 1 Scene 1?
questions.a: Her father Egeus orders her to marry Demetrius, but she loves Lysander; Athenian law threatens death or life in a convent if she disobeys, so she plans to run away with Lysander.

days.guide: Read Act 1 Scene 2 aloud in parts.

questions.q: What makes the mechanicals' scene funny?
questions.a: Bottom wants to play every role (even the lion, promising to roar 'as gently as any sucking dove'), Flute doesn't want to play a woman because he has 'a beard coming,' and Snug worries he's 'slow of study.'

days.guide: Read Puck's and Oberon's speeches; paraphrase three passages.

questions.q: Paraphrase Puck's 'I am that merry wanderer of the night.'
questions.a: 'I'm the fun-loving spirit who roams around at night (playing tricks).'

days.guide: The child completes the plot web and takes the terms quiz.

questions.q: What are the three groups of characters?
questions.a: The lovers, the fairies and the mechanicals (amateur actors).

weeks.assessment_key: Drama terms quiz: act, scene, dialogue, stage directions, monologue/soliloquy, aside, cast of characters, comedy. Plot web: three groups — lovers (Hermia, Lysander, Helena, Demetrius), fairies (Oberon, Titania, Puck), mechanicals (Bottom, Quince, Flute, Snout, Snug, Starveling) — linked by the woods outside Athens and Theseus and Hippolyta's wedding. 4 = all connections; 3 = one missing; 2 = groups only; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather: Folger text of the play, Lambs' Tales. Choose Act 3 scenes to read (Folger text). Keep the Week 26 lovers chart.
misconceptions: Forgetting why the love changes. The love-in-idleness flower's juice causes it.
Thinking the play-within-a-play is serious. 'Pyramus and Thisbe' is a tragedy performed so badly it becomes comedy.

days.guide: Read selected Act 3 scenes; chart who loves whom before and after.

questions.q: After both men are anointed, whom do Lysander and Demetrius love?
questions.a: Both love Helena; Hermia is left out.

days.guide: Read the Bottom/Titania scene aloud; find puns.

questions.q: What happens to Bottom, and what is funny about Titania's reaction?
questions.a: Puck gives him a donkey's head; enchanted, Titania falls in love with him and has fairies wait on him — the queen adoring a fool with a donkey head.

days.guide: Read Act 4 and the play-within-the-play in Act 5.

questions.q: How are the lovers' problems solved?
questions.a: Oberon has the spell removed from Lysander but leaves Demetrius loving Helena; Theseus overrules Egeus, and the two couples marry with Theseus and Hippolyta.

days.guide: Compare the Lambs' prose with the play; write two paragraphs.

questions.q: What is lost in a prose retelling?
questions.a: Shakespeare's poetry, wordplay, jokes and stage action — the mechanicals' comedy especially.

days.guide: Give the quiz and scene analysis.

questions.q: Who says 'Lord, what fools these mortals be!'?
questions.a: Puck.

weeks.assessment_key: Comprehension quiz: 1) Puck anoints Lysander by mistake, so he loves Helena 2) Puck gives Bottom a donkey's head 3) Titania, under the potion, falls in love with Bottom 4) Helena believes both men are mocking her 5) 'Lord, what fools these mortals be!' — Puck 6) Oberon releases Titania; lovers paired Lysander–Hermia, Demetrius–Helena 7) Theseus overrules Egeus 8) the mechanicals perform 'Pyramus and Thisbe' at the wedding. Scene analysis rubric: 4 = names the comic techniques (mistaken identity, wordplay, slapstick, dramatic irony) with quotes; 3 = one technique; 2 = summary; 1 = off-topic.

weeks.prep: Gather: scene script, simple costumes and props, filmed production clip. Find a filmed production clip (Globe on Screen or a free school production); collect simple costumes and props.
misconceptions: Reading Shakespeare's lines in a sing-song. Speak for meaning; let the rhythm support it.
Standing with back to audience; mark blocking.

days.guide: Watch a filmed scene and compare with the child's mental picture.

questions.q: What is a director's choice?
questions.a: Decisions about staging, costume, tone and movement that interpret the script.

days.guide: Cut a 2–3 minute scene, cast family and mark blocking.

questions.q: What is blocking?
questions.a: The planned movement and positions of actors on stage.

days.guide: Rehearse, tapping iambic rhythm; practice projection.

questions.q: What is iambic pentameter?
questions.a: A line of ten syllables in five pairs, each unstressed then stressed (da-DUM).

days.guide: Perform and record.

questions.q: Why face the audience when speaking?
questions.a: So they can hear and see expressions.

days.guide: The child writes a reflection and takes the unit test.

questions.q: Who is the queen of the fairies?
questions.a: Titania.

weeks.assessment_key: Performance rubric (4/3/2/1): lines learned; meaning clear; projection; gestures and blocking; teamwork. Reflection rubric: explains at least two choices with quotes. Unit test sample: Theseus/Hippolyta, the lovers' chart, Puck's mistake, Bottom's transformation, Pyramus and Thisbe, drama terms, iambic pentameter (ten syllables, da-DUM ×5).

weeks.prep: Gather: 'The Secret Garden' by Frances Hodgson Burnett (Project Gutenberg or library). Get The Secret Garden. Preview: chapter 1 opens with Mary's parents dying in a cholera outbreak in India; Burnett uses some colonial-era attitudes worth discussing.
misconceptions: Thinking Mary is simply 'bad'. Ask why: neglectful parents and servants who obeyed her every whim.
Skipping dialect. Read Martha's lines aloud — it gets easier.

days.guide: Read chapters 1–2; list traits and causes.

questions.q: Why is Mary so disagreeable at the start?
questions.a: Her parents ignored her and servants gave her whatever she wanted, so she never learned to care for others.

days.guide: Read chapters 3–4; describe the manor and moor.

questions.q: How does the setting reflect Mary's mood on arrival?
questions.a: The dark, gloomy manor and the bare, endless moor match her lonely, sour, cold feelings.

days.guide: Read chapter 5; translate dialect words.

questions.q: Translate Yorkshire dialect: tha', nowt, summat.
questions.a: you; nothing; something.

days.guide: Read chapters 6–7; predict.

questions.q: How does Mary find the key?
questions.a: A robin leads her to the spot where the buried key is in the earth.

days.guide: Write the character sketch; give the quiz.

questions.q: Why was the garden locked?
questions.a: Mr. Craven locked it after his wife died following an accident in it, ten years ago.

weeks.assessment_key: Character sketch rubric — 4: Mary's traits (sour, spoiled, lonely, curious) with three quotations, explanations of causes (neglect in India), and early signs of change; 3: two quotes; 2: list of traits; 1: off-topic. Quiz: 1) Mary's parents die of cholera in India 2) she is sent to her uncle Archibald Craven at Misselthwaite Manor in Yorkshire 3) Mrs. Medlock brings her 4) Martha is the maid 5) the garden has been locked for ten years 6) she hears crying in the corridors 7) a robin helps her find the buried key.

weeks.prep: Gather: The Secret Garden. Keep reading; let the child prepare three discussion questions.
misconceptions: Thinking the omniscient narrator is Mary. The narrator stands outside and sometimes comments directly.
Assuming Colin is simply sick. His fear and being treated as an invalid keep him weak.

days.guide: Read chapters 8–10; collect sensory images of the garden.

questions.q: How do the garden's changes mirror Mary's?
questions.a: As green shoots appear and she clears space, Mary grows stronger, healthier and kinder.

days.guide: Read chapters 11–12; analyze Dickon.

questions.q: What is special about Dickon?
questions.a: He is gentle, cheerful and at ease with nature; animals trust him, and people feel happy around him.

days.guide: Read chapters 13–14; compare Colin and early Mary.

questions.q: How is Colin like Mary at the beginning?
questions.a: Both are spoiled, unloved, lonely children used to giving orders and having their way.

days.guide: Read chapter 15; find narrator comments.

questions.q: What does an omniscient narrator do?
questions.a: Knows all characters' thoughts and can comment on events directly.

days.guide: Hold a book-club discussion; give the quiz.

questions.q: What does Mary ask her uncle for?
questions.a: 'A bit of earth' to plant seeds in.

weeks.assessment_key: Discussion rubric (4/3/2/1): prepared questions; cites text; listens and builds on others; respectful. Quiz: 1) Mary finds the door under the ivy 2) Dickon is Martha's brother who charms animals 3) Mary asks her uncle for 'a bit of earth' 4) Colin is Mr. Craven's son, who believes he will become a hunchback and die 5) Colin and Mary are alike: spoiled, lonely, demanding.

weeks.prep: Gather: The Secret Garden. Keep the novel; note chapter titles to help the child track events.
misconceptions: Thinking 'Magic' is supernatural spells. The children use it for the power of growth, belief and positive thinking.
Ignoring Mr. Craven's change. His healing completes the theme.

days.guide: Read chapters 16–19; analyze Mary's response to the tantrum.

questions.q: How does Mary's handling of Colin's tantrum show growth?
questions.a: She's still fierce, but she uses it to help Colin — checking his back and showing him he isn't becoming a hunchback; she cares about someone else.

days.guide: Read chapters 20–22; discuss the garden as a symbol.

questions.q: What does the garden symbolize?
questions.a: Healing and new life — as it comes back to life, so do the children (and later Mr. Craven).

days.guide: Read chapters 23–25; discuss 'Magic'.

questions.q: What do the children mean by 'Magic'?
questions.a: The power of nature, growth and positive thinking that makes things (and people) grow strong.

days.guide: Read chapters 26–27; compare ending and opening.

questions.q: How is the ending different from the opening?
questions.a: The book opens with death, neglect and a sour, lonely girl; it ends with healthy children, a reunited father and son, and a living garden.

days.guide: The child writes theme statements and takes the test.

questions.q: Who returns to the manor at the end?
questions.a: Archibald Craven, Colin's father.

weeks.assessment_key: Novel test: 1) Mary stops Colin's tantrum by scolding him and checking his back — there's no lump 2) Colin goes to the garden in his wheelchair 3) Ben Weatherstaff sees them; Colin stands up 4) 'Magic' = the healing force of nature and positive thinking 5) Mr. Craven dreams of his wife calling him to the garden and returns 6) Colin runs out of the garden into his father's arms. Theme statements (4 = two full-sentence themes with evidence, e.g., 'Nature and friendship can heal both body and spirit'; 'Thoughts and attitudes shape health').

weeks.prep: Gather: Secret Garden notes, computer. Gather Secret Garden notes and quote list.
misconceptions: Dropping a quote in as its own sentence. Embed it inside your own sentence with a lead-in phrase and follow it with analysis.
Switching to informal tone.

days.guide: The child writes a claim and gathers five pieces of evidence.

questions.q: Write a claim about who changes more.
questions.a: Example: 'Mary changes more because she transforms from a sour, selfish girl into someone who heals both Colin and the garden.'

days.guide: Teach embedding; the child drafts two body paragraphs.

questions.q: How is an embedded quotation different from a dropped-in quotation?
questions.a: An embedded quote is woven into your own sentence with a lead-in (e.g., 'When Mary first meets Colin, Burnett describes him as…') so it reads smoothly, and it is followed by analysis; a dropped quote stands alone as its own sentence with no introduction.

days.guide: Draft introduction, counterclaim and conclusion.

questions.q: Give a counterclaim to 'Mary changes more.'
questions.a: 'Some readers argue Colin changes more because he goes from bedridden to running.'

days.guide: Revise and edit; type the final.

questions.q: Make formal: 'Colin was totally being a brat.'
questions.a: 'Colin behaved in a spoiled, demanding way.'

days.guide: Submit with self-assessment; vocabulary test.

questions.q: What is a symbol?
questions.a: An object that stands for a bigger idea.

weeks.assessment_key: Literary argument rubric — 4: arguable claim (e.g., 'Colin changes more, because he moves from believing he will die to running'), 3+ embedded quotes with analysis, counterclaim and rebuttal, formal tone, varied sentences; 3: some analysis thin; 2: summary; 1: incomplete. Vocabulary test: novel and unit terms (symbol, theme, omniscient, dialect, characterization).

weeks.prep: Gather: library card, online databases (public library), Library of Congress and Smithsonian websites. Get a library card and log in to the library's databases; bookmark Library of Congress and Smithsonian sites.
misconceptions: Asking a too-broad question ('Egypt'). Focus: 'How did Egyptians move the stones to build the pyramids?'
Trusting any website. Check author, date, purpose and evidence.

days.guide: Brainstorm topics; the child narrows to a focused question.

questions.q: Make 'pyramids' into a focused research question.
questions.a: Example: 'How did ancient Egyptians build the pyramids at Giza?'

days.guide: Evaluate six websites with the checklist; keep three.

questions.q: Which is more reliable: a museum website or an anonymous blog?
questions.a: The museum website — known expert authors, purpose to educate.

days.guide: Visit the library; find a print book and database article.

questions.q: Why use a library database?
questions.a: Articles are from vetted, reliable publications.

days.guide: Model a paraphrased note card with source and subtopic.

questions.q: What should each note card include?
questions.a: A paraphrased fact, the source, the page/URL and a subtopic label.

days.guide: Build the works-cited list; refocus the question if needed.

questions.q: How are works-cited entries ordered?
questions.a: Alphabetically by author's last name (or title if no author).

weeks.assessment_key: Source evaluation sheets: each lists author, date, purpose and evidence with a keep/reject decision. Works cited: MLA format, e.g., Author Last, First. Title. Publisher, Year. — for websites include title of page, site name, date and URL; alphabetical by author. 4 = all sources correct; 3 = minor format errors; 2 = missing elements; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather: note cards, computer. Keep note cards organized by subtopic.
misconceptions: Copying sentences and changing a few words. That's still plagiarism; read, cover, write from memory, then cite.
Using one source per section. Synthesize at least two.

days.guide: Sort cards into subtopics; build an outline with headings.

questions.q: Why use headings in a report?
questions.a: They organize information and help readers find sections.

days.guide: The child drafts two sections synthesizing two sources each.

questions.q: What does 'synthesize' mean?
questions.a: Combine information from several sources into one explanation.

days.guide: Practice paraphrasing three passages; then draft the remaining sections with citations.

questions.q: How do you avoid plagiarism?
questions.a: Use your own words and sentence structure, quote exact words in quotation marks, and cite every source.

days.guide: Add intro, conclusion and a captioned graphic.

questions.q: What should a caption do?
questions.a: Explain what the graphic shows and how it relates to the text.

days.guide: Type the full draft; conference with the rubric.

questions.q: What is an in-text citation?
questions.a: A short reference in the sentence or parentheses, e.g., (Smith), showing the source of the information.

weeks.assessment_key: Draft check (research rubric): focused question answered; 3–4 sections with headings; each section uses 2+ sources with in-text citations; paraphrased; intro and conclusion; one captioned graphic; 3+ typed pages. 4 = all; 3 = one missing; 2 = several; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather: draft, slides or poster software. Set up slide or poster software.
misconceptions: Putting paragraphs on slides. Use images and key words; speak the details.
Rushing the talk. Practice with a timer.

days.guide: Revise for domain vocabulary and logical order.

questions.q: What is domain-specific vocabulary?
questions.a: Words specific to a subject, such as 'quarry' and 'limestone' for pyramids.

days.guide: Edit, check citations, publish.

questions.q: What should you check in every citation?
questions.a: That it matches a works-cited entry and the information really came from that source.

days.guide: Build 6–8 slides with images and minimal text.

questions.q: How much text should a slide have?
questions.a: A title and a few key words or a short phrase; the speaker explains.

days.guide: Rehearse a 5-minute talk.

questions.q: Name three speaking skills to practice.
questions.a: Eye contact, volume, clear pronunciation, pace.

days.guide: Present and answer questions.

questions.q: How should you answer a question you don't know?
questions.a: Say so honestly and offer to find out.

weeks.assessment_key: Report rubric — 4: accurate, well-organized, domain vocabulary, correct citations, few errors; 3: minor issues; 2: weak organization or citations; 1: incomplete. Presentation rubric — 4: 6–8 clear slides, 5-minute talk with eye contact, volume and clear pronunciation, answers questions with knowledge; 3: minor issues; 2: reads slides; 1: incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather: writing portfolio, summer reading list. Choose an unfamiliar short story and article (CommonLit) and a writing prompt with two short sources; gather the year's portfolio.
misconceptions: Answering constructed responses without evidence. Use the RACE frame: Restate, Answer, Cite, Explain.
Not planning timed essays. Spend 5 minutes outlining.

days.guide: The child reads an unfamiliar story and article and answers constructed responses using RACE.

questions.q: What does RACE stand for?
questions.a: Restate the question, Answer it, Cite evidence, Explain the evidence.

days.guide: Give a timed essay (about 45–60 minutes) with two sources.

questions.q: How should time be used in an on-demand essay?
questions.a: About 5–10 minutes planning, most time drafting, last 5 minutes rereading and fixing errors.

days.guide: Give the cumulative grammar and vocabulary test.

questions.q: Correct: 'Me and her read Hatchet.'
questions.a: 'She and I read Hatchet.'

days.guide: The child picks three pieces and writes a cover letter about growth.

questions.q: What makes a strong portfolio letter?
questions.a: Specific examples from the pieces showing growth, plus goals.

days.guide: The child makes a summer list of six books and gives a book talk.

questions.q: What should a book talk include?
questions.a: Title, author, a hook about the plot without spoilers, and why you'd recommend it.

weeks.assessment_key: Reading assessment: score each constructed response 2 = correct answer with text evidence explained, 1 = answer without evidence, 0 = incorrect. On-demand essay: use the argument or explanatory rubric (4–1). Grammar/vocabulary test sample: 1) 'between you and me' 2) 'he and I' 3) intensive pronoun: 'herself' 4) fix pronoun shift 5) fix vague pronoun 6) nonrestrictive commas 7) chron = time 8) metaphor vs simile 9) personification 10) connotation. Portfolio letter: 4 = three pieces with specific evidence of growth and goals.
